entry.dc:title: Statistical analysis of surface-water-quality data in and near the coal-mining region of southwestern Indiana, 1957-80
entry.dc:creator: Martin J.
entry.prism:publicationName: US Geological Survey Water Supply Paper
entry.dc:description: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act requires that applications for coal-mining permits contain information about the water quality of local streams. To meet this need for information, streamflow, specific conductance, pH, and concentrations of total alkalinity, sulfate, dissolved solids, suspended solids, total iron, and total manganese at 37 stations were analyzed to determine the spatial and seasonal variations in water quality and to develop equations for predicting water quality. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Comparison of some soil properties on natural and reclaimed hillslopes
entry.dc:creator: Toy T.J.
entry.dc:description: Handling of soil materials during surface mining may substantially modify their physical and chemical properties. In this report, a comparison is presented among: (1) bulk density, (2) particle-size distribution, (3) soil reaction, and (4) organic matter content of soils on natural and reclaimed hillslopes at the Dave Johnston Mine, Glenrock, Wyoming. At this site, no significant difference occurred in bulk density between the soils of natural and reclaimed hillslopes. No significant difference occurred in gravel content, but sand content was significantly higher on the soils of natural sites than on those of reclaimed sites. There were no significant difference in average pH between the soils of the natural and reclaimed hillslopes for the first decimeter of depth; however, the average pH of soils on the reclaimed hillslopes was significantly lower than those on the reclaimed hillslopes for the second, third, and fourth decimeters. Finally, no significant difference occurred in organic matter values between the soils of natural and reclaimed hillslopes for the first decimeter, but the difference was significant in the second decimeter. © 1987 The Williams & Wilkins Co.

entry.dc:title: Water prevention of the planned Vadna I open coal mine.
entry.dc:creator: Jeney Jambrik R.
entry.prism:publicationName: Acta Geodaetica Geophysica Et Montanistica Hungarica
entry.dc:description: Out of the characteristic five coal seams the lowest, developed in the Vadna brown coal territory belongs to the East-Borsod brown coal basin. This coal bed being near to the surface is planned to be mined with stripping in two parts. The hydrogeological and hydrological conditions of the territory are discussed in the paper, and a proposal is given for the protection of part 1 of the surface mining against surface and underground water.-from Author

entry.dc:title: LOW-FREQUENCY VIBRATIONS PRODUCED BY SURFACE MINE BLASTING OVER ABANDONED UNDERGROUND MINES.
entry.dc:creator: Siskind D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Report of Investigations United States Bureau of Mines
entry.dc:description: Bureau of Mines researchers assisted the U. S. Office of Surface Mining (OSM) by studying complaint-producing blasting vibrations resulting from an active surface mine operating over abandoned mine workings beneath the surface mine and the nearby town of Blanford, IN. Ground vibrations were of high amplitude and dominated by unusual and more structure response-producing low frequencies (4-8 Hz) than previous studies at other sites. These conditions resulted primarily from the geologic structure as the vibration propagating medium. Blast designs were partly responsible, with high level casting and complex multidelayed blasts producing wave interaction and constructive reinforcement. The traditional 8-ms criteria for separating charge weights per delay appears insufficient for this low-frequency site.

entry.dc:title: AUTOMATION, SIMPLIFICATION OF OPERATION AND INCREASE IN PERFORMANCE OF SELF-PROPELLED CONSTRUCTION AND SURFACE MINING MACHINES BY USE OF ELECTRONICS.
entry.dc:creator: Leidinger G.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the Iron and Steel Institute of Japan
entry.dc:description: The complexities of surface mining and construction machines have reached a degree at which operators are no longer in a position to operate them continuously in the most efficient way and guarantee full utilization of the available performance. It is necessary, therefore, to ease the operation, either by supplying the operator with information on the overall status of his machine or by giving him direct operating instructions. This information must be presented to the operator in such a manner that it requires only a small amount of attention. By the introduction of closed control circuits the operator can be partly - or in some cases entirely - relieved from the direction of certain functions of the machine. Increased efficiency by reductions in fuel consumption and maintenance is also made possible by improved machine monitoring techniques. These rely on the application of microelectronics in connection with variable hydraulic systems. The main emphasis of automation today is on these means of optimizing the performance of the machine.

entry.dc:title: Efficient Extraction of Brown Coal and other Raw Materials using Advanced Surface Mining Technology and Equipment under Different Conditions.
entry.dc:creator: Gerlach P.
entry.dc:description: The GDR covers 72% of its primary energy needs with brown coal. In 1985 it mined 312 Mt of lignite, i. e. 27% of world output. In view of the increasingly worsening conditions of brown coal quality and bedding, more complicated open-cast techniques and equipment is required. The article describes some of the open-cast mining operation under difficult geological conditions.

entry.dc:title: MINE-BUILT PONDS ECONOMICALLY CLEAR ACID MINE WATERS.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: One of the by-products of surface mining is acid mine drainage. Studies show that properly designed and constructed wetlands outfitted with cattails and other marsh plants can efficiently and inexpensively treat discharges of acid mine water. Wetland plants remove metals from acid water by adsorption (especially ion exchange); consumption (plant uptake); and simple filtration.

entry.dc:title: Reclamation planning for coal strip-mined lands in Montana
entry.dc:creator: Hall D.L.
entry.dc:description: Strip mining for coal is causing serious environmental problems in the coal-rich lands of Eastern Montana (U.S.A.). A comparison of surface-mine reclamation planning in the state of Montana and planning in other regions shows that local planning authority is relatively absent in Montana. Reclamation planning efforts in the United States have generally improved since passage of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 and since enactment of state reclamation laws. However, of the vast amounts of drastically disturbed land in Montana, only a small fraction has been successfully reclaimed. Local site-specific comprehensive plans may be essential for ensuring that the negative ecological and cultural impacts of strip mining are temporary. © 1987.

entry.dc:title: Subsea mineral resources.
entry.dc:creator: McKelvey V.
entry.dc:description: About 20 nonpetroliferous minerals are produced from the continental margins. Sand and gravel, lime from shells and aragonite mud, precious coral, and placer minerals, such as rutile, ilmenite, leucoxene, cassiterite, zircon, monazite, magnetite, gold, platinum, and diamonds are recovered by surface mining. Sulfur and salt are recovered by solution mining through drill holes. Barite is recovered by subsea quarrying. Coal and iron ore are mined underground from entry on adjacent land or from artificial islands. Potash is likely to be produced from subsea salt basins, and offshore production of phosphate is being considered in several areas. The resources of the deep-ocean floor are yet to be developed. Those drawing the most interest are manganese nodules and encrustations, metallic sulfide deposits, and red clays.-from Author

entry.dc:title: Optimization of overburden drill dust control systems on surface coal mines
entry.dc:creator: Zimmer R.A.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: A significant problem at U.S. surface mining operations is complying with more stringent dust standards resulting from high respirable free silica concentrations. In areas where potentially harmful concentrations of silica-bearing dust exist, more stringent dust standards are applied to limit the amount of respirable free silica to which the workers are exposed. According to U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) data, overburden drilling occupations have the greatest exposure to silica. Worker exposure may be reduced by reducing the amount of dust produced by the drill. This can be accomplished with either dry collection or wet suppression systems. Both of these systems were evaluated in the field, results of this testing are the subject of this paper. This work was performed under a U.S. Bureau of Mines contract by PEI Associates, Inc. A special study of dry and wet systems was conducted to determine the proper operating parameters for each type of system. Shroud height was evaluated for dry systems and water flow rate was evaluated for wet systems. In the case of dry systems, it was found that a nearly inverse relationship exists between shroud height and control efficiency. The dry system performed most efficiently when the shroud was positioned 0.23 m or less from the ground. In the case of wet systems, the control efficiency versus water flow rate curve showed a steep increase in efficiency in the range of 0.09 to 0.14 m3/hr. The highest control efficiency (96%) was at a water flow rate of 0.27 m3/hr. Flow rates this high however, can cause operational problems, such as plugging of the drill bit. In general, the results of the study demonstrated the efficacy of control equipment available in the U.S. for overburden drills. Used in combination, dust control equipment, pressurized cabs, and personal protective equipment should allow U.S. surface mine operators to comply with more stringent dust standards at surface coal mines. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: DISCUSSION ON A METHOD FOR DETERMINING THE CUTTING DRAG INDICES OF COAL AND ROCK.
entry.dc:creator: Liu Jinghui
entry.prism:publicationName: Meitan Xuebao Journal of the China Coal Society
entry.dc:description: This paper discusses the cutting drag indices, which represent the cutting characteristics of coal and rock in China, and several methods for determining these indices by taking into consideration the measured cuting drag of in-situ coal and rock in mines and the mining technology of surface mining, rock properties, rock cutting drag and design calculation of selected excavators, etc. After deduction and analysis, the paper introduces four indices, namely the average cutting drag, K//c//l, peak value average cutting drag, K//F//c//l; quadratic equivalent cuting drag, K//2; peak value maximum cutting drag, K//m//a//x, for representing the cutting characteristics of coal and rock. A first attempt is made of using this method for predicting the cutting drag of brown coal in Zhaotong in Yunnan Province.

entry.dc:title: Environmental benefits of surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Grimshaw P.N.
entry.dc:description: Most forms of economic activity affect the environment in ways which can be claimed to be detrimental. Some of the worst results were produced in the past by mining. However, handled correctly, surface mining can have beneficial effects and the author discusses this, taking examples from coal mining activities in Great Britain.

entry.dc:title: EVALUATION OF SELECTED PIT CONFIGURATIONS FOR SURFACE MINING A MODERATELY PITCHING COAL SEAM.
entry.dc:creator: Chugh Y.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
entry.dc:description: The objective of this study was to conduct a technical and economic evaluation of selected pit orientations in mining a single seam dipping at 8. 53 degree (15%) to a maximum depth of 46 m (150 ft). Such mining conditions are prevalent in the Hanna Coal Basin in Wyoming. The evaluation emphasized the effect of pit orientation on overburden stripping operations since it constitutes the major portion of the mining cost. The study utilized physical models of the mining systems with different pit orientations, a dragline simulation model developed by Fluor Mining and Metals (1981), the Open Pit Material Handling Simulation Model (OPMHS), and a surface mine cost model (COSTMOD) developed by Manula et al. (1976).

entry.dc:title: ANALYSIS OF COAL SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT IN ILLINOIS.
entry.dc:creator: Bhagwat S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
entry.dc:description: Equipment capacities of sample of Illinois surface coal mines representing about 60% of surface production in the state were studied. Available equipment capacity was compared with the required capacity as indicated by coal production and stripping ratios reported. Most mines sampled showed surplus equipment capacity, which if avoided, would result in cost savings. The surplus capacity results mostly from market fluctuations that result in underutilization of equipment. Study findings underline the importance of market assessment at the time of mine planning.

entry.dc:title: PROBLEMS IN RECLAIMING STRIPPED MINED TUNDRA LANDS ON THE NORTH SLOPE, ALASKA.
entry.dc:creator: Bandopadhyay S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
entry.dc:description: The coal resources of the North Slope can be expected to attract interest because the nearly flat-lying coal beds are especially amenable to surface mining. Mining on a scale large enough to justify coal development in this area could have severe environmental effects. The mitigation would be uncertain because large-scale coal mining and reclamation operations have not been carried out in the arctic. The objective of this paper is to establish the interrelationship between the problems due to permafrost and factors in reclamation of post-mining land in order to suggest reclamation approaches that may be appropriate in this region.

entry.dc:title: SELECTION OF EXPLOSIVES FOR SURFACE MINING INDUSTRY - A CRITIQUE.
entry.dc:creator: Ghose A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: This paper seeks to address the methodology of explosive selection based on an appraisal of the current state-of-the-art of the theory and practice of explosive usage in surface mining industry. Limited results from studies carried out in India are also presented to underscore the feasibility of the approaches. Additionally, the need for a purposive rock mass classification, based on field data of explosive utilization, is outlined.

entry.dc:title: REDUCTION OF QUARRYING COST THROUGH USE OF CRUSHER/BELT CONVEYOR SYSTEMS.
entry.dc:creator: Mueller G.
entry.dc:description: In the 1950s the German cement industry was the first to develop crusher/belt conveyor systems. Handling rates of 250 tph and sizes of less than 50 mm did not present any problem for rubber belt conveyors. By 1975 conveyor installations capable of handling 1000 tph and by 1980 of 2000 tph were available. While the impetus to these development efforts emanated from the cement industry where limestone is the raw material, crusher/conveyor systems made their appearance in 1975 in the surface mining of bauxite and phosphate and, in 1980, copper ore. In 1986, Krupp Industrietechnik GmbH will supply the first 6000 tph mining system for iron ore. It will be commissioned in Australia. This article discusses mobile crushing plant markets, costs, and other aspects of the subject.

entry.dc:title: Use of hold-gro erosion control fabric in the establishment of plant species on coal mine soil
entry.dc:creator: Day A.D.
entry.dc:description: Experiments were conducted on the Black Mesa Coal Mine, Kayenta, Arizona in 1977 and 1978 to study the effectiveness of Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric (a product from the Gulf States Paper Corporation, Tuscaloosa, Alabama) in the establishment of plants on coal mine soil following the surface mining of coal. Four plant species were planted: (1) spring barley (Horduem vulgare L.), an annual grass (2) crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum L.), a perennial grass (3) alfalfa (lucerne) (Medicago sativa L.), a perennial legume and (4) fourwing saltbush (Atriplex canescens Pursh.), a perennial shrub. Seeds of each plant species were planted in reclaimed coal mine soil in the spring of the year by both broadcast seeding (conventional culture) and the incorporation of seeds in Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric. Average numbers of seedlings established and percent ground cover for all species studied were higher in areas where conventional culture was used than they were in areas where seeds were incorporated in Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric. The incorporation of seeds in Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric in the establishment of plant species on coal mine soil was not an effective cultural practice in the southwestern United States. © 1986 Science and Technology Letters.

entry.dc:title: GROUNDWATER RECOVERY PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH OPENCAST MINE BACKFILLS IN THE UNITED KINGDOM.
entry.dc:creator: Reed S.M.
entry.dc:description: The paper presents the main findings of the research work conducted over the past three years into the environmental effects associated with surface mining. Especial considerations have been given to the re-establishment of the natural groundwater regime, as a consequence of opencast site restoration. A summary of the results of the research is presented and two specific topics, namely, the stability of backfilled masses and the pollution of groundwater, are detailed. The project was based on field and laboratory investigations, and details of this work along with some general conclusions are given.

entry.dc:title: IMPROVED BLAST DESIGNS CAN REDUCE ROCKFALL HAZARDS.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: The most serious hazard in surface mining is falling rock from high-walls. Looking for ways to improve high-wall stability, the Bureau of Mines evaluated blasting practices at several surface coal mines. In most cases, blasting practices contributed to highwall instability. Improved blast designs reduced highwall overbreak through simple changes in the timing blasts that changed the direction and time of burden movement.

entry.dc:title: SHIFTABLE BELT CONVEYORS IN SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Increasing demand for bulk materials such as ore, coal, lignite, oilsand, oilshale and bauxite has led to more opencast operations, where huge amounts of overburden and partings must be transported by conveyors, trucks or trains. Shiftable belt conveyors have proved to be versatile and economical in many such applications.

entry.dc:title: INCO'S NEW OPEN PIT DELIVERS LOW-COST NICKEL ORE.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Filling the processing pipeline with lowcost mined nickel ore was Inco's main motive for developing its new Thompson open pit mine in northern Manitoba, Canada. The new pit, which mines the crown pillar of the Thompson underground mine, replaces ore that was previously railed from the Pipe open-pit, located 20 min to the south. The decision to bring the Thompson open-pit mine into production rather than rejuvenate or develop any of the other underground mines was based primarily of the fact that surface mining technology, personnel, and equipment already existed at the Pipe open pit. Mining is carried out in the pit two shifts/day operating on 45-ft benches with 25-ft berms. The ultimate dimensions of the mine will be 5,100 ft along the north-south direction, 800 ft in the east-west direction, and 400 ft below surface at its deepest point.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING OF COAL . . . GROWTH THROUGH EVOLUTION.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: Starting with primitive steam shovels and converted dredges and fostered by ability of American manufacturers to build larger, powerful stripping machines, surface mining of coal advanced from modest beginnings 75 years ago to reach its dominant role today. But although the age of big strippers is still here, smaller, more versatile equipment is coming on the scene.

entry.dc:title: WESTERN SURFACE MINING: OUTSTANDING TECHNICAL ISSUES.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Research could resolve most of the uncertainties about Western surface mine reclamation, and could increase the probability of reclamation success with fewer design problems and lower costs. However, cutbacks in Federal funding have significantly reduced reclamation research. The Office of Surface Mining's inflexible application of some reclamation standards also has inhibited the adoption of innovative reclamation methods. This article discusses some of the outstanding technical issues involved, including acid potential in Western mine spoils, sediment control, revegetation, and others.
